title: Simple Arabic Pronunciation
summary: A gentle first introduction to a few Arabic sounds that don't exist in English, and how to approach learning them without pressure.

body.text: The Quran was revealed in Arabic, and the core wording of Salah stays in Arabic across the whole Muslim world — the practical benefit is that a Muslim from Indonesia and a Muslim from Nigeria can pray side by side using the exact same words. That's also why learning a handful of Arabic sounds is genuinely useful early on, even before you're fluent in anything else.
A few sounds that don't exist in English

Arabic has some letters that don't map onto any English sound, which is exactly why transliteration (writing Arabic in Latin letters) is only ever an approximate bridge, not the real thing. A few worth knowing about early:

• ع (ain) — a sound produced deep in the throat, often transliterated as a plain "a" but genuinely distinct from it.
• ح (ha) — a breathy "h" from further back in the throat than the English "h."
• ق (qaf) — a deep "k" sound made further back in the throat.
• ط / ص / ض (ta, sad, dad) — "emphatic" versions of t/s/d, pronounced with more weight and a lower tone.

You don't need to master these to start — just knowing they exist helps explain why a word can look one way in transliteration but sound noticeably different from what an English reader expects.
How Muslims have protected this for 1,400 years

There's an entire traditional science, called Tajweed, dedicated purely to correct Quranic pronunciation — where to lengthen a sound, where to soften it, exactly how each letter should be produced. This level of care exists because the Quran has always been transmitted primarily by listening and repeating after a teacher, generation after generation, not just by reading text off a page. That's also the most effective way for you to learn it: listening to audio recitation repeatedly (available throughout this app's Quran section) and trying to imitate it, rather than trying to sound it out from transliteration alone.

body.question: Do I need to learn the whole Arabic language to pray properly?
body.answer: No — praying only requires a small, fixed set of short phrases (opening chapter, a short surah, and some fixed phrases for bowing and prostrating), which is a very different, much smaller task than learning conversational Arabic. Many lifelong Muslims never become fluent Arabic speakers while still praying correctly every day.

body.question: How long does it realistically take to get comfortable?
body.answer: It varies hugely by person, but most new Muslims report feeling reasonably comfortable with the required prayer phrases within a few weeks to a couple of months of regular practice — and comfort keeps improving for years after that. There's no deadline, and reciting a phrase imperfectly while genuinely trying is described in Islamic teaching as still rewarded, not penalised.
